items.title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum - Chapter IV
items.description:
The Wonderful Wizard of Oz is an American children's novel written by author L. Frank Baum. It is the first novel in the Oz series of books. A Kansas farm girl named Dorothy ends up in the magical Land of Oz after she and her pet dog Toto are swept away from their home by a tornado Upon her arrival in Oz, she learns she cannot return home until she has destroyed the Wicked Witch of the West.

The ground-breaking success of both the original 1900 novel and the 1902 Broadway musical prompted Baum
items.why_watch: This is a straightforward audiobook reading of Chapter IV of Baum's classic, useful if you're revisiting the original text alongside a child or refreshing your memory before a deeper read. With only 64 views, it's a quiet, no-frills recording — don't expect production polish. Best suited for listeners who want the source material without commentary or dramatization.

items.why_watch: Artem Kirsanov, a Harvard neuroscience PhD student, walks through his actual Zettelkasten setup in Obsidian with the kind of clarity that comes from someone who thinks rigorously about how knowledge compounds. What sets this apart from the crowded Obsidian tutorial space is his emphasis on the *why* behind each structural choice, not just the how. global_silver_linings.reason: Sometimes the most hopeful thing we can do is pause, reflect, and consider the bigger picture of our lives — and a thoughtful horoscope column has been inviting people to do exactly that for decades. There's quiet comfort in any practice that encourages self-awareness and a sense of possibility.

discovery_articles.title: Mysteries of the commonplace
discovery_articles.snippet: Editor in Chief Nancy Shute reviews new research in static electricity and other science revelations in our September magazine issue.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Static electricity — the thing you've been casually blaming for bad hair days since childhood — turns out to harbor physics we still don't fully understand. There's something quietly humbling about science admitting the sock-and-carpet phenomenon isn't fully solved.

garden_note.note: The dahlias are having their absolute moment right now in Zürich, their heavy heads nodding in the warm August dusk as the light softens to honey — go out and deadhead a few before the evening cools completely. Late summer here carries that bittersweet edge: the garden is lush and generous, yet you can just feel September waiting quietly in the wings.
